With an aging grid and a wave of incoming data centers, could schools help solve North Carolina’s energy crunch? Sustainability think tank Frontier Group and advocacy group Environment North Carolina released a report that found that the state’s schools could host 900 megawatts of solar energy. That’s enough to power all the homes in a Durham-sized city, or 150,000 homes.

The report’s authors analyzed aerial photos of school roofs across the state. They totaled at least 1,300 football fields worth of unoccupied rooftop real estate. If filled with solar panels, that much energy would offset a little more than 1% of North Carolina’s annual power needs.

text:
A state representative who has successfully sponsored legislation expanding nuclear energy in Arkansas said he will sponsor another bill next year that will fund the state’s dormant “atomic coordinator” role.

Rep. Jack Ladyman, R-Jonesboro, said he would seek to pass a version of a bill recommended in a study presented to lawmakers Aug. 6 by EXCEL Services Corporation, a nuclear energy consulting company. Lawmakers commissioned the study through Act 707 of 2025, which Ladyman sponsored.

It recommended lawmakers pass what it called the Arkansas Nuclear Competitiveness Act. Its provisions would include expanding the atomic coordinator’s duties and providing staff support. The position was created in the 1950s but was never filled. The suggested bill among other provisions would define nuclear energy as clean energy and align Arkansas law with federal programs, allowing the state to apply for federal grants.

Ladyman, an engineer, said he had a lengthy career in the energy industry that included working 30 years for GE. He served as a regional manager in charge of environmental health and safety over all GE power plants operating west of the Mississippi River and in Canada.

Ladyman believes Arkansas can be a leader in the nuclear energy industry. It already is home to one of the nation’s 57 nuclear power plant locations, which is Arkansas Nuclear One operated by Entergy near Russellville. Arkansas Tech University offers an associate of science in nuclear technology degree. Nuclear energy has the support of local communities, and the Legislature has passed three bills and three resolutions that Ladyman has sponsored.

“I don’t know of anybody in the Legislature that has come to me and talked to me negatively about nuclear power,” he said.

Arkansas was one of 28 states that responded to a U.S. Department of Energy request for information for its Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus program. Such campuses would be created through federal-state partnerships and would encompass nuclear power’s entire life cycle from mining to recycling.

It was not one of 12 selected for the next round or one of five that signed memorandums of understanding in July. The five – Tennessee, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Idaho and Utah – will continue exploring becoming host sites for the campuses.

However, Arkansas was one of six other states invited to attend a recent Energy Communities Alliance meeting in Chicago along with the final five. The six could partner with those states in the future.

Ladyman said nuclear power can help address the expected significant increase in energy usage in the coming decades. That increase is coming as a result of increased use by data centers, crypto mines, electric vehicle operators, population growth and other consumers. He noted that the state at the same time is losing two coal plants, and the two Arkansas Nuclear One reactors are aging.

He said nuclear energy can produce large amounts of electricity without emitting carbon dioxide, and the energy can be stored. Unlike solar and wind energy, it can produce energy continuously.

But nuclear power plants have had their own challenges, including the possibility of a meltdown and the creation of radioactive spent nuclear fuel rods that are stored on site.

Ladyman said newer, smaller nuclear reactors address these issues. Parts for Generation IV small modular reactors can be produced in a factory, so there are fewer cost overruns. New designs would prevent meltdowns by allowing the reactors to be cooled using liquid metal such as lead rather than water.

Also, a nuclear innovative campus can recycle and reprocess spent nuclear fuel rods. While old plants like Arkansas Nuclear One use 5% of the available energy and leave 95% as waste, just the opposite is the case with new technology, and the waste can be further recycled.

title: Regulators Roundtable: Documents reveal GOPAC's secretive influence network for utility ...
description:

In April 2025, the Regulators Roundtable hosted a series of dinners on the sidelines of the Current Issues Conference, a utility industry gathering at New Mexico State University in Santa Fe.
A political arm to support member commissioners Unlike NARUC and other organizations that bring state regulators together, the Regulators Roundtable has a component explicitly for spending on electoral politics.

Following the January 2026 Washington, D.C. meeting, Regulators Roundtable PAC hosted a “campaign school” for member commissioners.
text:
A recent Washington Post investigation brought new attention to the Regulators Roundtable, a little-known organization that connects Republican state utility commissioners with companies and trade associations that have interests before the regulators, and raises money from those companies and groups.

The Energy and Policy Institute provided records to the Post revealing how the organization solicited utilities and industry groups to become “investors” during its early formation. Some regulators and industry representatives told the Post that the group exists for educational purposes.

The records show that the Regulators Roundtable is more than a forum for exchanging ideas. EPI has filed more than 200 public records requests seeking to understand the Regulators Roundtable’s operations and structure, its relationship with GOPAC, the Republican organization that houses it, and its work on energy policy.

Since 2025, the Regulators Roundtable has built a network of entities, including a political action committee to defend Republican commissioners in elections and an affiliated media platform that publishes utility and energy-related articles and op-eds. It has organized private meetings between regulators and corporate “investors,” helped commissioners communicate with the Trump administration, drafted policy comments, provided political and communications training, and advanced the interests of incumbent fossil generators and monopoly utilities.

A new “subgroup of GOPAC”: the creation of the Regulators Roundtable

GOPAC is a Republican down-ballot political training organization founded in 1978 that describes itself as “the Republican Party’s premier organization for educating and electing a new generation of leaders.” The group operates a network of entities, including a political organization known as a “527” group, which can raise and spend unlimited funds to influence elections.

GOPAC launched the Regulators Roundtable in January 2025. Roundtable President and GOPAC board director Elizabeth Gianini later explained to North Carolina Utilities Commissioner Tommy Tucker that the idea came from Oklahoma Corporation Commission Chair Kim David, who had been active in GOPAC as a state senator and “felt like there is not a place where conservative commissioners could get to know each other, share best practices and hear about current and cutting edge technology from a business perspective.”

David, who had served on GOPAC’s Legislative Leaders Advisory Board since 2017, was the Regulators Roundtable’s 2025 advisory board chair.

On January 10, 2025, three days before Gianini’s start date at the Roundtable, GOPAC Chairman David Avella emailed Gianini and David a “roster of Energy CEOs in Oklahoma as a resource for your fundraising.” Gianini replied that her priority was to “get a name and a mission statement for the organization.”

The organization eventually took shape through several entities: the 501(c)(3) Regulators Roundtable Institute; the 501(c)(4) Regulators Roundtable Inc.; and the Regulators Roundtable Political Action Committee. A GOPAC-affiliated outlet, Policy Platform News, also launched a website with energy-focused articles and opinion columns, Energy Platform News.

By May 2025, then-Arizona Corporation Commission Chair Kevin Thompson described the Roundtable as a “subgroup of GoPAC.” Gianini also wrote to North Dakota Public Service Commissioner Jill Kringstad that she was “excited you wanted to join the Regulators Roundtable” and was “working with GOPAC to see when they are offering their next campaign training in DC, and get you scheduled to attend that too.”

Records also show that the Roundtable recruitment drew on Georgia Public Service Commissioner Tricia Pridemore’s position as president of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC) at the time. Pridemore was an early Roundtable member, received emails addressed to members of the Roundtable’s Advisory Board in March 2025, and appeared on guest lists for an April dinner with potential “investor” companies. Gianini and David also appear to have used several NARUC conferences as opportunities to recruit regulators.

Pridemore also helped Gianini connect with potential new members. Gianini emailed Wyoming PSC Chair Mike Robinson in January 2026 “to follow up on a conversation with Pridemore, who shared that you expressed interest in joining a future Regulators Roundtable Institute meeting.” Gianini met with Robinson on the sidelines of NARUC’s 2026 Winter Policy Summit and later emailed to welcome him to the Roundtable.

At least 19 regulators from 12 states were listed in event materials as attendees of GOPAC or Regulators Roundtable events examined by EPI in 2025 and early 2026, while records connect several additional commissioners to the organization.

Investors receive access to commissioners, counter “liberal organizations”

While Gianini, Pridemore, Thompson, and David worked to recruit member regulators, the Roundtable representatives also sought funding from potential corporate donors. In April 2025, the Regulators Roundtable hosted a series of dinners on the sidelines of the Current Issues Conference, a utility industry gathering at New Mexico State University in Santa Fe.

Ahead of the conference, Gianini sent David a detailed briefing email identifying the “investors” and regulators scheduled for meetings, along with information about the prospective investors and an investor prospectus.

For $50,000, the “inaugural member investor” was offered access to commissioners at an “exclusive” two-night inaugural event in Phoenix, a two-day GOPAC energy workshop in Nashville that also included legislators, access to future meetings in 2026, and opportunities to submit content to the Energy Platform News website. The prospectus also said that, in fall 2026, donors who contribute over $5,000 to the 501(c)(4) group or the PAC would receive a fall election briefing with “key Commissioners on the ballot.”

Several companies with interests before regulators, or trade associations representing them, have supported or participated in the Roundtable. The Washington Post reported that the American Gas Association and the Nuclear Energy Institute were among its investors. Google’s head of state legislative affairs, Ron Barnes, sits on the Roundtable Institute board, and Gianini described Google in one email as a “great supporter from the start of our organization.”

Other board members across the Roundtable network work in lobbying, government affairs, or industries affected by utility regulation, according to documents obtained by EPI:

Peter Horkan, a partner at the Caravel Group, a Nashville-based consultancy, who is also a board member of GOPAC’s 527 organization;

Mike Huebsch, a former Wisconsin Public Service Commissioner who made headlines for approving projects proposed by Dairyland Power Cooperative before resigning and applying for the cooperative’s CEO position;

Jimmy Glotfelty, a former chair of the Texas Public Utility Commission and current government affairs employee for Aalo Atomics, a company developing small modular reactor technology;

Mike Nasi, a partner with Jackson Walker LLP and adviser for coal advocacy organizations Life:Powered and Energy Policy Network;

Brian Sailer, a registered lobbyist for the firm Flywheel Government Solutions whose 2025 clients included Bloom Energy, a fuel cell manufacturer.

In an email inviting Southern Company executives to a Roundtable dinner, Gianini described one of the Roundtable’s objectives as countering “liberal organizations” that were “advocating against conservative commissioners,” such as incumbent GOP commissioners on the Arizona Corporation Commission.

A May 2025 member newsletter similarly said the Roundtable “exists to equip and support conservative, both elected and appointed, commissioners with the knowledge, strategy, and network they need to push back” on “liberal environmental groups pushing a 100% green energy agenda.”

The records also show that Roundtable officials paid close attention to state transparency requirements, and perceived them as a potential risk. In her email outlining the Santa Fe meetings, Gianini told David she was “getting nervous about the ‘noticing requirements’” in different states and asked whether those rules could make meetings open to the public or press. “State by state I need to resolve that before we have more than one from a state on the RR Advisory Board,” she wrote.

Gianini also told Kringstad that “due to your notice rules, you and Commissioner Haugen-Hoffart will have to most likely rotate coming to the meetings.”

The Roundtable also communicated with regulators via personal email accounts. In one case, Gianini obtained a personal email and cellphone number for Mississippi Commissioner Wayne Carr’s administrative assistant.

Gianini even asked Idaho PUC Commissioner Ed Lodge, the Roundtable’s 2026 chair, if he wanted to remove a list of new member states from an internal email “if you have a concern about FOIAs.”

Carrying a “PSC perspective” to the Trump administration

The Roundtable has also sought to give member commissioners a coordinated voice in federal energy policy–one that is outside NARUC’s existing committee structure for representing state regulators in Washington.

In July 2025, Gianini drafted a memo to Stephen Moore, a former economic adviser to President Trump and then an economist at the Heritage Foundation. Moore is now a senior fellow at the America First Policy Institute. The memo sought to convey a “PSC perspective” on policies intended to “move faster” to build new power generation.

Thompson, the Arizona regulator, asked Gianini to modify the memo to call for rolling back six categories of EPA regulations that he said were “adding costs onto our ability to use natural gas and coal fired generation.” All six of Thompson’s requested rollbacks appear in a later copy of the memo, which urged the administration to “revitalize coal,” treat natural gas as a “clean and strategic fuel,” extend incentives to gas infrastructure and expand pipeline capacity.

After securing Thompson’s approval, Gianini sent the memo to Oklahoma’s David, Louisiana PSC Commissioner Eric Skrmetta, and Nebraska PSC Commissioner Kevin Stocker. Stocker responded, “I really like the commonsense elements of this.”

In another case, records indicate that Gianini and a lobbyist, Shawn Day, helped prepare and submit comments under the signatures of state commissioners to the Justice Department’s Anticompetitive Regulations Task Force docket. The comments urged the DOJ not to target the vertically integrated utility model. The final filings did not identify the Roundtable’s role.

Three versions were submitted to the docket, all of which list “Elizabeth Gianini” under the “Submitter Name” field on regulations.gov. Two included PDF files whose embedded metadata listed “Elizabeth Gianini” as the author. Metadata for a fourth version posted by GOPAC-linked outlet Energy Platform News listed Day as the author.

Pridemore, then president of NARUC, circulated the comments to other commissioners while making clear the effort was “not affiliated with NARUC.” She urged her colleagues to sign the comments to counter what she described as “grossly negative comments and pressure” regarding “our commissions and state utilities” from “NGOs trying to push us into full deregulation or worse.”

NARUC maintains a committee for engaging federal policymakers. Its Washington Action Program exists to provide a “framework for improving the credibility, visibility, and effectiveness of NARUC in Congress, the Executive Branch, the media, and other stakeholder organizations.” NARUC separately submitted its own comments in the docket, which Pridemore signed in her capacity as the association’s president.

The Roundtable has also facilitated access to current senior federal officials.

In November 2025, members participated in a virtual meeting with Peter Lake of the White House National Energy Dominance Council about potential federal rules governing the interconnection of large electricity users such as data centers.

Months later, the group hosted its second major Roundtable meeting at a luxury hotel one block from the White House. Commissioners and private-sector sponsors met with officials from the White House, Department of Energy, Environmental Protection Agency, and Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Lake also led a separate “commissioner only briefing” with the National Energy Dominance Council.

Communications support and shaping media coverage

At the October 2025 Roundtable, GOPAC Chairman David Avella led a communications session offered “exclusively to commissioners” to help raise their public profiles through social media and op-eds. The communication support extended to helping commissioners produce the content itself.

Records show that Gianini and lobbyist William Greener of Greener and Hook LLC drafted a pro-coal, anti-renewable op-ed for Nebraska PSC Commissioner Kevin Stocker. Energy Platform News later published a nearly identical version under Stocker’s name.

Another record revealed that Gianini drafted a document for Idaho Commissioner Ed Lodge to criticize renewable energy and defend vertically integrated monopoly utilities. The Idaho PUC’s public information officer told EPI that “Commissioner Lodge didn’t pursue [the op-ed] further or sign off on it.”

The Roundtable and Gianini promoted additional commissioner-bylined op-eds on social media, including pieces attributed to David, Thompson, Pridemore, Skrmetta, Georgia Commissioner Fitz Johnson, Mississippi Commissioners Chris Brown and Wayne Carr, and North Dakota Commissioner Sheri Haugen-Hoffart.

The Roundtable’s communications network also extended beyond Energy Platform News (EPN). The site, operated by Policy Platform News, described itself as an “independent U.S. media organization” without disclosing its ties to GOPAC. But Policy Platform’s parent organization, Policy Platform Inc., was incorporated at the same address and with the same registered agent as the Regulators Roundtable Institute, while records show Policy Platform staff using gopac.org email addresses.

A Roundtable newsletter described EPN as one of two media platforms the organization supported for conservative commissioners and identified Day, the lobbyist, as Policy Platform’s editor. Day is a registered lobbyist for an LS Power subsidiary. He was also listed as the media contact for the Mountain Valley Pipeline, which EPN covered favorably.

One of Day’s colleagues at his Richmond-based firm, Capital Results, partner Wayne “Jabo” Covert, sits on GOPAC Inc.’s board. The firm also lobbied in 2025-26 for energy companies, including EQT, Colonial Pipeline, NextEra Energy, Old Dominion Electric Cooperative, and Washington Gas.

The Roundtable offered corporate investors access to the publication. Its investor prospectus said companies contributing $50,000 would receive opportunities to submit material to Energy Platform News during 2025 and 2026.

The site published a number of articles and editorials that offered favorable coverage of the gas industry, including an op-ed titled “If you like food, then you should like natural gas” by Pickering Energy Partners’ Dan Romito.

Other headlines included “American coal is cleaner than Chinese wind and solar,” “Lay all Biden energy credits on the chopping block,” and “Net zero does not facilitate return on investment,” as well as at least two columns from Alex Epstein, who denies the dangers of climate change.

EPN published a three-part exclusive interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright focused on the Trump administration’s energy policies, including its efforts to end DEI initiatives, expand private energy development, and reverse climate policies. Wright was interviewed by Dan Haley, a former CEO of the Colorado Oil and Gas Association whom EPN identified as a Policy Platform board member.

EPN also published at least five other editorials by Roundtable member commissioners, including three members of the Arizona Corporation Commission.

Sometime between August 3 and August 15, 2026, all content was removed from Policy Platform’s and EPN’s websites. The Washington Post ran its story on the Roundtable on August 12.

A political arm to support member commissioners

Unlike NARUC and other organizations that bring state regulators together, the Regulators Roundtable has a component explicitly for spending on electoral politics.

The Regulators Roundtable PAC endorsed candidates for elected utility commissions, contributed directly to their campaigns, and provided political training.

Gianini told Southern Company representatives, including then-Senior Vice President of Federal Regulatory Affairs Noel Black, that the group aimed to counter organizations opposing conservative utility commissioners.

Gianini told Wyoming PSC Chair Mike Robinson in June 2025 that the PAC was focused on defending Georgia Republicans and “strong pro-business” incumbents in Arizona.

After Republicans lost two Georgia Public Service Commission seats in November 2025, Gianini told Roundtable member commissioners: “We lost 2 great PSC members last week, and cannot afford to lose anymore!” She also wrote an EPN op-ed arguing that the results represented a “strategic breakthrough” for the “Green New Deal movement,” as “groups tied to the League of Conservation Voters, EarthJustice, Michael Bloomberg’s Carbon Fund, and Hollywood activist Jane Fonda spent millions of dollars… campaign[ing] with feelings, not facts.”

Days after the Georgia PSC election, the Roundtable’s 501(c)(4) group posted a job advertisement for a full-time finance director who would work “under … the GOPAC Network Finance Director.”

The Regulators Roundtable PAC subsequently became active in several states with elected utility commissions, with contributions to candidates in Georgia and North Dakota, and endorsements of candidates in both states, as well as Arizona, Alabama, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and South Dakota.

The PAC’s website also published an attack ad, paid for by Conservative Grassroots Network Election Fund, targeting Arizona Corporation Commission candidate Ralph Heap, who challenged Thompson and Myers in the Republican primary. The week before the primary, Thompson posted a photo of himself and Myers attending GOPAC- and Roundtable-sponsored events in Florida. Heap defeated Myers in the primary.

Campaign finance filings show money moving in both directions. Ahead of the 2025 Georgia PSC election, the Regulators Roundtable PAC received a $25,000 contribution from “Gas South PAC Inc.,” the PAC of a Georgia-regulated gas marketer. In March 2026, after Pridemore announced a run for Georgia’s 11th Congressional District, her state campaign committee, Georgians for Pridemore Inc., donated $197,194.82 to the Regulators Roundtable PAC. (Pridemore was legally barred from transferring funds from her PSC campaign, a state committee, to her federal campaign for the U.S. House.)

The GOPAC Election Fund later endorsed Pridemore for Congress. The fund spent a total of $289,960 on independent expenditures to support her federal campaign. The fund also reported $14,000 in “printing/canvassing” independent expenditures supporting Kim David’s 2026 congressional campaign. Both Pridemore and David failed to advance to the runoff in their respective GOP primaries.

Following the January 2026 Washington, D.C. meeting, Regulators Roundtable PAC hosted a “campaign school” for member commissioners. Sessions covered fundraising, polling, campaign messaging, grassroots organizing, media strategy, and the use of artificial intelligence in political communications. Presenters were largely national Republican political operatives, including veterans of Americans for Prosperity and the Republican Governors Association, as well as a representative from YouTube, a subsidiary of Google, an inaugural Roundtable investor.

Who attended, what it cost, what was disclosed

Documents show at least 19 regulators from 12 states appear on invites or attendee lists for the April 2025 Santa Fe dinners, July 2025 Nashville workshops, or the October 2025 and January 2026 Roundtables:

Note: Iowa Utilities Commissioner Josh Byrnes was included on a guest list for a Santa Fe meeting, but Byrnes confirmed to the Washington Post that he did not attend any Roundtable events.

Records connect at least nine additional regulators to the group. Gianini described Oklahoma’s Brian Bingman as a member, while emails show Wyoming’sMike Robinson, North Dakota’s Jill Kringstad, and Texas’ Thomas Gleeson agreed to join. Emails further show that unnamed commissioners from Texas, Indiana, and Vermont had registered for the July 2026 Roundtable.

Alabama’s Jeremy Oden and South Dakota’s Kristie Fiegen signed the Anticompetitive Regulations Task Force comments. Oden and Florida’s Mike La Rosa also received materials from the November 2025 virtual meeting. Oden, however, told the Post that he did not participate in any Roundtable meetings or calls.

Financial and ethics records show that GOPAC and the Regulators Roundtable spent thousands of dollars per public official at some events, including more than $1,000 per attendee on food and drink in some cases.

Arkansas commissioners Doyle Webb and Katie Anderson disclosed $2,810.90 and $2,662.91, respectively, in expenses paid by the Roundtable for the October 2025 Scottsdale meeting.

For the January 2026 Washington, D.C. meeting, North Carolina’s Tommy Tucker received complimentary meals worth $1,034.85, flights worth $502.83, and lodging worth $738.54, according to an email sent to Tucker and two members of his staff by a Roundtable consultant.

North Carolina requires officials to report scholarships over $200–defined to include travel, lodging, and meals–on annual Statements of Economic Interest when out-of-state entities provide them. Tucker’s staff flagged the requirement before the D.C. meeting, writing that they need to “collect the full cost associated with Commissioner Tucker’s attendance at this event or any events he’s attended this past year that was covered by your group.”

North Carolina Utilities Commission budget authorization forms also characterized Tucker’s attendance as official commission business and identified the Roundtable as the source of funding. For the Scottsdale meeting, Tucker wrote that he was traveling to “represent the Utilities Commission of North Carolina” and the organization would reimburse all related costs. Emails indicate that Gianini booked Tucker’s flight for the Nashville conference.

Tucker’s 2025 disclosure forms, however, do not disclose any such scholarships.

Louisiana’s Skrmetta does not appear to have filed any disclosures corresponding to the hospitality he received at these events in the Louisiana database either, despite Louisiana requiring a “public servant” who accepts “complimentary admission, lodging, or transportation” to file Form 413 with the Louisiana Board of Ethics within 60 days.

Utility contributions to GOPAC accelerate

Much of the financing behind the Regulators Roundtable and the broader GOPAC network is opaque, since 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4) entities are not required to disclose donors. But utility contributions to GOPAC Inc., the 527 political arm, are public, and have significantly increased in recent years–surging from an average of around $61,000 per year in the 2010s to $795,000 in 2024 and $940,000 in 2025.

That money largely leaves the 527 entity for electoral use: 76.5%, or $38,563,310, went to the GOPAC Election Fund between Q1 2021 and Q2 2026. The GOPAC Election Fund, in turn, transferred almost 80% of its funds to state-level Republican political organizations.

As utility giving accelerated, GOPAC’s 501(c)(3) Education Fund hosted an energy-specific workshop in Nashville in July 2025.

Several members of GOPAC’s Legislative Leaders Advisory Board, including Wisconsin Assembly Majority Leader Tyler August and Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, were asked to nominate “appropriate committee chairs or influential committee members” for the events to foster discussion with “public policy experts and industry influencers.”

At the Nashville conference, North Carolina’s Tucker, Oklahoma’s David, and Arizona’s Thompson gave a presentation titled “Powering America Forward: PSCs and Legislators United for Energy Dominance.”

Other sessions featured Moore, the former Trump adviser, who reiterated longstanding anti-renewable talking points; Pickering Energy Partners’ Dan Romito, who touted fossil fuels (while bashing Democrats with outlandish, seemingly AI-generated cartoons); the fossil fuel and utility front group Consumer Energy Alliance; and nuclear reactor manufacturer Westinghouse.

description:
Solar power is now the cheapest form of energy on Earth, with solar panel prices having plummeted an astonishing 90 percent since 2010.
While richer nations initially led the charge for solar power capacity additions, poorer nations are now representing an increasingly considerable share of demand growth.
While this raises some concerns for energy security, cheap and abundant Chinese solar panels have made the worldwide solar revolution possible.
Finally, solar power is no longer a matter of climate policy – it’s a matter of energy security and simple economics.
In fact, ironically enough, Donald Trump is currently overseeing the biggest expansion of solar power in United States history.
text:
Solar power is far and away the world’s fastest-growing form of energy production, beating out every other form of energy on Earth in 2025. Despite a recent political pivot away from renewable energies in the world’s largest economy, solar power additions continue to shatter its own records year over year as the sector has long since outgrown any need for subsidies. Solar power has simply become too cheap to fail.

“We have a plentiful and cheap source of electricity that can be built quickly, almost anywhere in the world,” NewScientist wrote in an article published late last year. “Is it fanciful to imagine that solar could one day power everything?”

How has a once-niche and costly form of energy generation taken over the global economy in under 30 years? According to a new report from Scientific American, solar’s stunning success story comes down to four interrelated factors: affordability, policy, fossil fuel leapfrogging, and the finite nature of fossil fuels.

Solar power is now the cheapest form of energy on Earth, with solar panel prices having plummeted an astonishing 90 percent since 2010. This newfound affordability has led to an enormous uptick in photovoltaic installations in nearly every corner of the globe. While richer nations initially led the charge for solar power capacity additions, poorer nations are now representing an increasingly considerable share of demand growth. In countries where national power grids are unreliable or limited and power is costly, solar-plus-battery systems represent an affordable and secure alternative. Pakistan, for example, has become an unexpected poster child of solar adoption in recent years as residents install rooftop solar and batteries faster than any other market on Earth.

This rapid decline in costs has evolved thanks to early policy pushes from two vastly different economies and governments – China and Germany. According to Scientific American, in the early 2000s “the German Green Party leveraged a power-sharing arrangement to demand subsidies for rooftop solar” at the same time that China was undertaking a massive effort to expand its manufacturing capacities. “The German subsidies helped to create a European market for solar modules and components, and Chinese firms built factories to meet that demand,” the article argues.

China still dominates the solar manufacturing sector today, controlling a whopping 80 percent of global supply chains. While this raises some concerns for energy security, cheap and abundant Chinese solar panels have made the worldwide solar revolution possible. And that solar revolution has been of utmost importance in many developing countries that are being tasked with the difficult imperative of leapfrogging straight over fossil fuel development and straight into clean energy buildout.

Finally, solar power is no longer a matter of climate policy – it’s a matter of energy security and simple economics. While commitment to climate goals is intermittent, whipsawing between political administrations, energy security strategy is evergreen – and solar now represents the clearest pathway forward to energy autonomy and resilience. Ongoing volatility in global oil and gas markets driven by the United States’ and Israel’s war in Iran (on top of drawn-out supply chain complications from Russia's war in Ukraine) has catalyzed a global embrace of solar power as a central part of energy security strategy.

“Wind and solar cannot be embargoed, blockaded, or shut off by a foreign power,” David Frykman, General Partner at Stockholm-based venture capital group Norrsken, wrote in an op-ed for Fortune earlier this year. “Every terawatt-hour of domestic renewable generation is a terawatt-hour that no adversary can weaponize.”

As a result of these four factors, it’s clear that the solar power revolution is here to stay, even as administrations come and go. In fact, ironically enough, Donald Trump is currently overseeing the biggest expansion of solar power in United States history.

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

text:
Electric cooperatives on Wednesday continued urging the Environmental Protection Agency to fully repeal a 2024 rule regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, pointing to the harm it would inflict on electric affordability and reliability as demand climbs.

The Biden administration rule remains the law of the land today and restricts operations at existing coal-fired plants and new natural gas facilities unless they install carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) technology that is not commercially available or technically feasible, co-op leaders say.

The 2024 rule “puts utilities in an untenable position where they invest significant dollars into new power plants that they are then restricted from running at full capacity,” NRECA CEO Jim Matheson said during an Aug. 19 media teleconference. “That doesn’t make sense.”

The Trump administration issued a proposal in June 2025 to roll back the requirements but has yet to finalize it. Matheson urged the agency to finalize a complete repeal of the 2024 rule immediately.

“We need a full and complete repeal,” he said.

Under the Biden rule, if new combined-cycle gas plants do not install CCS by 2032, they would be forced to shut down.

Between now and 2032, new combined-cycle gas plants must meet emissions limits that cannot be achieved by the majority of new plants, which means they will be limited to running at 40% of their potential output. Simple-cycle plants similarly must meet emissions limits that cannot be achieved by most new units or be limited to running 20% of the time.

Consequently, the rule could force the construction of duplicative gas plants to equal the output of a single plant that is allowed to run near full capacity, co-ops say.

Generation and transmission co-op leaders on the call pointed to projects already under development, emphasizing that the rule increases costs and complicates long-term planning just as demand rises from residential and industrial growth and new data centers.

Oglethorpe Power Corp., based in Tucker, Georgia, is building two combined-cycle gas facilities and two gas peaking units over the next seven years, with the first combined-cycle facility totaling $3.3 billion. Together, these new generation investments will represent the most efficient gas generation in Oglethorpe’s fleet.

But unless the 2024 rule is repealed, that highly efficient capacity would be forced to sit idle 60% of the time, requiring Oglethorpe’s members to spend an additional $150 million to $300 million per year on replacement power, President and CEO Annalisa Bloodworth said.

“Georgia’s cooperatives and Oglethorpe care deeply about our communities and their success,” she said. “For more than 50 years, we’ve taken care of our environment, we’ve significantly reduced our emissions, and we have kept the lights on. But we cannot do that at a price consumers can afford with the deeply flawed mandates of this rule.”

“A full repeal of the power plant rule is what we need. It is critical to be able to plan, to invest with confidence and to protect Georgians from senseless costs that they can’t bear,” Bloodworth said.

David Tudor, CEO and general manager of Associated Electric Cooperative, which serves member-consumers in Oklahoma, Missouri and Iowa, said his G&T is building five combustion turbine peaking units to meet rising demand from households and in anticipation of higher demand from manufacturing and data centers.

But average earnings for the co-op’s consumer-members is $50,000 a year, which “puts a lot of pressure on us to keep electric rates affordable.”

“We’ve got to keep our existing fleet to keep the lights on … and then we’re having to build a new generation to meet the load growth,” Tudor said. “To be told at the last minute, while we’re already under construction, that we can only operate these plants at 20%-40% is just silly.”

“There are so many flaws in the rule; it needs to go away,” he concluded.

Todd Brickhouse, CEO and general manager of Basin Electric Power Cooperative in North Dakota, said the country’s energy independence hinges on the cost and availability of energy.

But the 2024 power plant rule “adversely impacts both of these.”

Basin Electric is building the $4 billion, 1,490-megawatt combined-cycle Bison Generation Station and recently completed a 580 MW natural gas generating facility consisting of simple-cycle generators and reciprocating engines. Although renewable energy makes up 30% of the co-op’s portfolio, “to bring electrons onto the grid rapidly, it’s all a natural gas game right now,” Brickhouse said.

Earlier this week, the North American Electric Reliability Corp., the nation’s grid watchdog, predicted the U.S. will need around 200 gigawatts of additional power within seven years, equal to the demand of about 200 San Franciscos.

Co-ops are making thoughtful investments and long-term plans for new generation, and “the sooner we can take away this major uncertainty and absurd restriction on our ability to run these plants, the better,” Matheson emphasized.

“There’s such a focus on affordability these days,” he continued. “Electric cooperatives serve 92% of all the persistent poverty counties in America—affordability is front of mind for every co-op across the nation. The best policy action we can take today to address affordability is repeal this rule.”

description:
So a developer in Fresno skipped it, laid the panels flat on the ground, and has now published five months of output.
That is a strange omission for a performance release, and it makes 862 MWh unreadable on its own.
Hitting 101 percent of a P50 model tells you the model was built for a flat array in Fresno and the array is meeting it.

text:
Ground-mount solar has a steel problem. You buy the modules, then you buy tons of structural steel to hold them at an angle, then you pay a crew to drive posts into graded dirt and bolt the whole thing together.

On a small municipal project, that middle layer is often what decides whether the numbers work at all. So a developer in Fresno skipped it, laid the panels flat on the ground, and has now published five months of output.

ForeFront Power says the array has run at an average of 101 percent of its expected production since late March and delivered 862 megawatt-hours to the city, per its August 13 announcement carried by CleanTechnica. Every outlet that picked it up ran the same two numbers.

Neither of them tells you what you probably want to know, which is whether flat beats tilted. So let’s work that out.

Start with the size, which nobody printed

The announcement never states how big the array is. That is a strange omission for a performance release, and it makes 862 MWh unreadable on its own.

The number exists in older coverage. When the Fresno Department of Public Utilities portfolio was finished, a project FAQ put the Northeast Surface Water Treatment Facility at 1.7 MW-DC with 1 MW-AC and 2 MWh of Sungrow battery storage.

Run the arithmetic on that. From late March to August 13 is about 141 days. 862 MWh across 1.7 MW-DC works out to roughly 3.6 kilowatt-hours per installed kilowatt per day, and that is over spring and early summer, the best stretch of the year in the Central Valley.

Now the benchmark. The same DPU portfolio, 27 MW-DC across three sites, is projected to generate about 47 million kWh a year. That is around 4.8 kWh per kilowatt per day as an annual average, winter included.

Beating your own model by one percent proves less than it sounds

So the flat array is delivering roughly three quarters of what the portfolio it belongs to was designed to average, and it is doing it during the sunniest months on the calendar. The real annual gap is wider than that comparison makes it look.

Some of that is not about tilt. Solar Power World reported at the portfolio’s completion ceremony in April 2025 that the DPU projects used single-axis trackers, and a tracker beats fixed-tilt before you even get to the flat-versus-angled argument.

Which is the point. Hitting 101 percent of a P50 model tells you the model was built for a flat array in Fresno and the array is meeting it. It does not tell you flat-mount closed the gap on tilt, because the gap was priced into the forecast before anyone poured a foundation.

Treat the 1.7 MW figure with a little care, since it comes from 2025 coverage of the wider portfolio rather than from this month’s release, and the Erthos build reached commercial operation almost a year after the ceremony that declared the portfolio done. If the site’s capacity changed in between, the yield math moves with it.

None of this makes the project a failure. It makes it a cost story rather than a performance story, which is exactly how Erthos has always sold it.

Steel and civil work were the two lines that killed the math

Fresno did not do this to make a point about the future of solar. It did it because a conventional array stopped penciling.

ForeFront approached Erthos in 2023, after inflation and supply shocks pushed labor and material prices up far enough to wreck the payback period. Erinne Davis, a senior project manager at ForeFront, told Solar Builder the design let them skip “significant, expensive civil upgrades” on top of the racking steel and the labor to install it.

Skipping the grading is arguably the bigger win. Erthos says its arrays follow contours up to a 15 percent slope, so the bulldozers that normally flatten a lot before construction starts never showed up. In California, that phase is where schedules and budgets tend to bleed.

The density claim is the other half. Flat panels do not shade each other at low sun angles, so there is no row spacing, and Erthos puts the gain at up to 275 percent more energy per acre or up to 60 percent less land for the same interconnect capacity.

Fresno owns none of it. The city buys the power under a 20-year PPA at a fixed rate below what the utility charges, with ForeFront owning and maintaining the assets at no upfront cost and no bond money.

Worth noting how the deal got done, because that is the replicable part. Fresno procured through the Renewable Energy Aggregated Procurement program, a pre-negotiated public-sector contracting vehicle run by SPURR. And the labor Erthos supposedly eliminates was still union: the DPU sites were built by IBEW Local 100.

Heat is the objection, and Tyler answered it years ago

Everyone who looks at flat-mount solar raises soiling first. Tilted panels get rinsed by rain and shed dust downhill, flat ones do not, and Fresno sits in an agricultural basin that produces real summer dust.

Erthos handles that with a robot. The ErthBot is a dry nylon brush unit that runs at night as needed, covers more than 3.5 MW-DC per machine, and parks itself at a charging dock before the sun comes up so it is never shading production.

The economics of it are more persuasive than the press-release adjectives. Erthos chief executive Jim Tyler has put the comparison at roughly 50 cents per kW to clean a tracker plant once, against cleaning an Erthos plant “every day for a year for 50 cents per kW”. Dry brushing also uses no water, which in California is not a small detail.

The objection almost nobody raises is temperature. Silicon loses efficiency as cell temperature climbs, and a module lying on hot ground gets less rear convection than one sitting on a rack in open air.

Tyler says he checked. In the same interview he described running a fatal-flaw analysis on the concept, deciding temperature was the only serious candidate, and then operating an early plant in Phoenix through 118°F ambient without cell temperatures approaching their maximum.

Durability got a harsher test in Chowchilla, about 40 miles north of Fresno, where an Erthos array sat through a California winter of atmospheric rivers, bomb cyclones and 80-mph gusts, as Canary Media reported after visiting the site.

Erthos is seven years old and now chasing data centers

The company is based in Tempe, Arizona, and Tyler founded it in 2019 after a career on the build side. He ran the EPC team at First Solar, then co-founded Depcom, a solar EPC outfit that grew large enough for Koch Industries to buy it.

Funding has been modest by cleantech standards: a $17.5 million Series B in March 2022 led by Capricorn Investment Group, then a $24 million round in 2023. TIME named it to a list of America’s top greentech companies this April.

The strategic move worth watching came in March, when Erthos announced a formal push into the AI data center market as a full energy solutions provider rather than a mounting vendor. That is a crowded room, but the pitch translates: operators already building their own generation behind the fence care about dollars per megawatt-hour and acres per megawatt more than they care about racking philosophy.

Tyler framed the Fresno result in exactly those terms, saying the design can “unlock projects that might otherwise be constrained by conventional construction costs.” Not projects that produce more. Projects that get built.

What the next twelve months actually decide

Five months is a start, not a record. The interesting data has not arrived yet.

Winter is the first real test, because that is when a zero-tilt array in the northern hemisphere gives up the most against a tracker, and Fresno sits near 36.7 degrees north. The second and third summers are the other one, once soiling patterns settle and the ErthBot has to earn its keep across years rather than months.

If the flat array holds its model through a full winter, ForeFront has something more useful than a press release. It has a public reference asset with a public number attached, in a state where every water district in the Central Valley has the same problem Fresno had.

That buyer profile is already well established. Water and wastewater plants own fenced acreage, run around the clock and carry ugly power bills, which is why they keep turning up in odd solar experiments, including the California operators floating panels over irrigation ponds because the only flat ground left was planted.

Which is the honest read on this. Nobody in Fresno proved flat panels out-generate tilted ones, because they do not. What got proved is that a 1.7-megawatt array can be cheap enough without the steel that a city signs a 20-year contract it would otherwise have walked away from, and for a municipal budget that is the only comparison that ever mattered.

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Growth Energy, the nation’s largest biofuel trade association, commended the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today for issuing a temporary emergency fuel waiver that clears the way for the continued sale of E15, a fuel blend made with 15% ethanol that costs less than standard fuel and is approved for use in 96% of cars on the road today.

E15 requires a waiver from the EPA in order to be sold in the summer. The agency has been issuing these emergency waivers consistently since May, and today’s announcement supports continued E15 availability across the U.S. for the remainder of the summer driving season.

“Today’s announcement aligns with this EPA’s track record of giving retailers the certainty they need to keep E15 on the market all year long,” said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor. “Now we need Congress to follow suit by passing legislation to permanently allow year-round E15 every year. Retailers, farmers, and drivers shouldn’t have to rely on EPA to provide separate waivers each year in order to have access to this more affordable fuel option. We applaud EPA for taking this initiative, and hope Congress does the same when it returns from recess by getting year-round E15 to the president’s desk.”

Environmental Defense Fund filed a lawsuit today challenging the Trump administration’s attempt to eliminate climate science functions at the National Center for Atmospheric Research.

The Trump administration’s unlawful attack on NCAR’s climate research functions would limit our understanding of how climate change puts Americans in harm’s way.

(BOULDER, Colo.) Environmental Defense Fund filed a lawsuit today challenging the Trump administration’s attempt to eliminate climate science functions at the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and to close the iconic Mesa Laboratory where NCAR is headquartered.

NCAR is a world-renowned institution for Earth system science research, including on climate change, and its cutting-edge models are used to power tools that help Americans prepare for and respond to climate disasters like worsening fires, hurricanes and flooding. The Trump administration’s unlawful attack on NCAR’s climate research functions would limit our understanding of how climate change puts Americans in harm’s way.

“When we check the weather or track the path of a hurricane, we’re leaning on science generated by the National Center for Atmospheric Research,” said Erin Murphy, Lead Counsel, Clean Air and Energy Markets at Environmental Defense Fund. “The federal government’s investment in climate science plays a critical role in our ability to understand and prepare for more frequent and intense extreme weather events caused by climate pollution. The Trump administration is attempting to eliminate NCAR’s vital climate science research and close its Mesa Laboratory at a time when Americans everywhere are suffering from the impacts of climate change, including more intense heat and fires, more dangerous floods and storms, and skyrocketing insurance costs.”

In December 2025, White House budget director Russell Vought announced in a social media post that the “National Science Foundation will be breaking up the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado.” He later stated that the administration plans to “fully close” the Mesa Lab.

NCAR was founded in 1960, with primary support from the National Science Foundation, and aims to “achieve excellence in United States science” and to “promote the discovery, integration, dissemination, and application of new knowledge in service to society.” Congress has since directed NSF to specifically support research that helps us understand how climate change impacts people and the planet. The Trump administration is acting unlawfully in its attempt to unilaterally eliminate climate research at NCAR without seeking any public input.

Environmental Defense Fund’s lawsuit also challenges the Trump administration’s unlawful failure to assess impacts and conduct a public consultation process before attempting to close — and potentially sell off — the Mesa Laboratory. This public process is required under the National Historic Preservation Act due to the Mesa Laboratory’s architectural significance and the history of notable scientific discoveries made there.

description:

text:
The Strait of Hormuz crisis is a reminder of how exposed the global energy system remains to geopolitical disruption. It is not a new problem. COVID-19, the Russia-Ukraine war, and conflicts in the Middle East have each revealed the same structural vulnerability: dependence on imported fossil fuels carries real and recurring costs.

74% of the world’s population live in countries that are net importers of fossil fuels, with developing countries particularly exposed. While 655 million people remain without electricity and 2 billion still rely on polluting fuels for cooking, every price spike widens import bills and drains scarce foreign exchange, competing directly with the investment needed to expand electricity access and clean cooking. Countries in this position have limited room to absorb shocks.

A structured response

The solution to this could be promoting more in-country energy generation.

The logic is straightforward: a country generating its own solar or wind power is not exposed to supply disruptions originating thousands of kilometres away.

The development of Energy Transition and Investment Plans (ETIPs), which are country-owned frameworks that help governments move from fossil fuel dependence toward domestically produced clean energy, could be a key starting point.

By identifying priority sectors and technologies, shaping investment pipelines, and translating transition commitments into concrete plans, ETIPs can help countries reduce import dependence, direct investment where it is most needed, and build more resilient energy infrastructure.

Country-level evidence

The savings, as evidenced by the ETIPs that SEforALL has helped develop, are substantial. In Barbados, where fossil fuels account for 91% of electricity generation, the ETIP projects BBD 15.6 billion (7.8 billion USD) in fuel cost savings by 2035. Ghana’s ETIP targets a ~90% reduction in domestic oil and gas consumption, saving approximately USD 180 billion in fuel costs by 2060. Sierra Leone’s ETIP is projected to deliver USD 4.7 billion in import savings, with green hydrogen replacing fossil fuels from 2040. At the largest scale, Nigeria’s shift to domestic renewables is projected to generate USD 686.8 billion in fuel cost savings by 2060 according to its ETIP.

These projections depend on infrastructure delivery. Nigeria’s ETIP targets 277 GW of total installed capacity and over 104,000 mini-grids by 2030. Sierra Leone’s ETIP allocates USD 5.5 billion for grid upgrades and storage critically in a system where 46% of electricity is currently lost in distribution.

Southeast Asia

The region warrants particular attention. The Philippines sourced 95% of its crude imports from Gulf countries; Vietnam 88%, Malaysia 69%, Thailand 59%, Singapore 52%, Indonesia 20%.

At the same time, the region is projected to account for more than 25% of global energy demand growth by 2035. Electricity demand has more than doubled in two decades, growing at around 3.3% annually, with fossil fuels absorbing the vast majority of that growth. Without structural change, growing demand will increase rather than reduce the region’s exposure to supply disruptions.

SEforALL is currently developing an Energy Transition and Investment Roadmap for the ASEAN region, working with member states on a shared approach to energy security.

Covering power, transport, industry, buildings and agriculture, the roadmap identifies where domestically and regionally generated clean energy can displace imported fossil fuels and quantifies the investments needed to enable that transition.

As ASEAN Member States rely on many of the same fuel suppliers, they share common energy security risks. Strengthening cross-border electricity interconnections allows surplus renewable generation in one country to meet demand in another, enhancing energy systems reliability and resilience in ways that national planning alone cannot achieve. This is where regional planning matters, and what the ETIR is designed to support.

The region is also well positioned to strengthen its role in clean energy value chains. ASEAN holds nearly half of the world’s nickel reserves and around one-fifth of global rare earths reserves - critical inputs for batteries, wind turbines, electric vehicles, and other clean energy technologies. By developing domestic and regional value chains, ASEAN can capture greater economic value, create new industries and jobs, and reduce dependence on imported clean energy equipment, rather than simply replacing fuel imports with technology imports.

The case for planning now

Emergency measures address immediate shortfalls. Transition plans address the underlying structure. The technology and financing mechanisms to build more resilient energy systems are available. The constraint is usually planning capacity and investment coordination, which is precisely what ETIPs are designed to support.

SEforALL invites governments and partners to engage with the ETIP process.

text:
New houses, including row houses and town houses, aren’t far behind: In 2025, 48% were built with heat pumps, up from 45% in 2024.

The stats are the latest evidence that heat pumps are taking over the U.S. residential heating market. For the past four years, these devices have outsold conventional gas-fueled furnaces, which belch pollution that endangers health and warms the planet. The tech’s growing popularity is a positive sign for decarbonization, since burning fossil fuels in buildings contributes nearly a tenth of the nation’s total greenhouse gas emissions.

The data reveals another piece of good news: The majority of all homes built last year — 78% of new apartment units and 56% of new houses — had electric heating in some form, either heat pumps or less-efficient electric-resistance systems.

This trend toward electric heating has persisted for over two decades now, across federal administrations, though it varies regionally. For example, in the South, with its milder winters, 96% of new apartments are electrically heated; in the Northeast, it’s just 52%.

Driving the shift to heat pumps is likely a combination of factors, according to Alan Durning, executive director of the Sightline Institute, a sustainability nonprofit in the Northwest. The two that stand out, he said, are improvements to the technology and the increased demand for air conditioning during climate change–fueled heat waves. While heat pumps are pricier up front than gas furnaces, they can be competitive with a gas furnace plus central AC.

A federal tax credit expanded under the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act could have also spurred heat-pump installations. That incentive offered developers up to $5,000 per energy-efficient housing unit. But even though the credit expired last month after being axed by President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress, developers still stand to profit by ditching gas in new buildings.

All buildings require electrical infrastructure. But hooking up to a gas pipeline on top of that adds complexity, time, and expense. New Mexico land developer John Moscato says that by skipping gas-line construction, his company reduces costs by $3,000 per lot. That adds up fast.

“In our upcoming development of 4,500 lots, we expect the savings of being all-electric to be approximately $13.5 million,” Moscato said.

Some states, like California, Colorado, and Washington, have standards that encourage new construction to go fully electric. But ​“red states are never going to pass laws requiring a phaseout of gas in new buildings,” Durning said.

Still, he said, policies that simply boost new housing in such states can move the needle toward cleaner buildings, since developers are increasingly likely to opt for electric heating appliances. And unlike gas bans, these laws are politically palatable, he added, pointing to recent pro-housing zoning reforms passed in deep-red Montana and Idaho. ​“We are getting accidental electrification,” he said.

Some legislators may ​“say climate change is a hoax, but they want to free the market in their cities to build more housing,” Durning said. ​“In red states, building more apartments will move us closer to decarbonization.”

text:
LG Energy Solution has started production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells at its all-new, 226-acre facility in Lansing.

The plant plans to reach more than 35GWh of annual battery-making capacity at full-scale production.

“Today marks a defining milestone for LG Energy Solution,” says David Kim, CEO of LG Energy Solution. “Lansing will produce advanced batteries that support not only the future of mobility, but also America’s growing energy infrastructure and digital economy. The facility’s LFP battery cells for energy storage systems are integrated by LG Energy Solution Vertech, the company’s U.S. energy storage division, into complete systems for utility, grid-scale storage, and other commercial and industrial applications.

Unlike many other high-tech industries, battery making creates jobs for everyone, from hourly workers to advanced degree holders.”

LG Energy Solution Michigan-Lansing also will produce more energy dense nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cells for Toyota. The cells will power battery electric vehicles like the 2027 Toyota Highlander EV, which will be assembled at Toyota Motor Manufacturing Kentucky (TMMK) in Georgetown, Ky.

title: Restoring cuts to two USDA programs will help more farmers adopt regenerative agriculture - EWG
description:
When federal conservation programs have adequate funding, more farmers sign up and put the money toward the most environmentally beneficial and cost-effective regenerative agriculture practices.
Independent analysis has found between 70% and 120% higher profitability(link is external) for farms that adopt regenerative agriculture practices and a return on investment of 15% to 25% over 10 years.
Restoring funding for EQIP and CSP could help more farmers adopt practices that should also help secure their future financial stability.
They are vital to helping farmers adopt regenerative agriculture practices.
Farm bill conservation cuts would hurt farmers The upcoming farm bill must maintain conservation funding, especially for regenerative practices.
text:
When federal conservation programs have adequate funding, more farmers sign up and put the money toward the most environmentally beneficial and cost-effective regenerative agriculture practices.

But these programs are in danger of even more cuts.

House and Senate Republicans are floating farm bill proposals that would further reduce funding for the Agriculture Department’s Environmental Quality Incentives Program, or EQIP, and Conservation Stewardship Program, or CSP.

The bill as written would leave(link is external) more than 56,500 valid farmer applications unfunded by EQIP over the next few fiscal years. The key states set to be hit hardest by estimated cuts and unfunded valid contracts are:

Arkansas – $81.6 million and 2,232 contracts

Alabama – $35.9 million and 2,171 contracts

Kansas – $51.6 million and 1,593 contracts

West Virginia – $17 million and 661 contracts

Georgia – $62.8 million and 2,411 contracts

Colorado – $56.5 million and 822 contracts

Regenerative agriculture practices such as cover crops and riparian buffers can help increase farm resilience and profitability while also improving the environment. Although they need reform, these programs help reduce agriculture’s air and water pollution, and add to farm resilience.

Independent analysis has found between 70% and 120% higher profitability(link is external) for farms that adopt regenerative agriculture practices and a return on investment of 15% to 25% over 10 years. Restoring funding for EQIP and CSP could help more farmers adopt practices that should also help secure their future financial stability.

Preventing those cuts could provide tens of thousands of farmers with continued support for vital conservation projects. Two amendments to the draft farm bill, offered by Sens. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), would restore funding to the programs.

If Congress adopts either amendment, significantly more farmers would receive EQIP and CSP support than they would under the current Republican bill.

EQIP and CSP funding

In 2024, nearly $1.9 billion in USDA conservation support went to practices that increase regenerative agriculture. But as available funding shrank, in 2025, federal support for those regenerative practices dropped by more than $1 billion.

As money for these popular programs disappears, fewer and fewer farmers are able to receive the support they need. In contrast, when funding is available for these programs, existing participants put more funding into good practices and more farmers are able to take part.

The EQIP and CSP are two of the largest federal conservation programs. They are vital to helping farmers adopt regenerative agriculture practices.

The White House’s own Make America Healthy Again strategy highlighted(link is external) the importance of expanding the two programs:

Empowering farmers and keeping solutions voluntary by expanding programs like the Environmental Quality Incentive Program and Conservation Stewardship Program, all while avoiding burdensome mandates; [and] keeping decision-making local and practical with solutions from the farm, not Washington, D.C.

Despite the Trump administration strategy, the House-passed farm bill and the Senate version under consideration would cut the two programs by over $2.4 billion.

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA, included billions more dollars for EQIP and CSP as an opportunity for farmers and ranchers.

Before the IRA funding, just 31% of applicants received(link is external) an EQIP contract, leaving a backlog of thousands of farmers and ranchers. Following the IRA funding, 43% of farmers(link is external) received EQIP funding for 2024.

States had made progress with the IRA funding in eliminating a backlog of applications – and the additional funding inspired more farmers to apply.

All farmers and ranchers, regardless of what they grow or where they live, are eligible for conservation funding. That means the farmers who grow fruits and vegetables – the food that the dietary guidelines for Americans and doctors tell us to eat – are more likely to get this money than traditional subsidies.

Farmers of color, beginning farmers and women are also much more likely to receive EQIP and CSP funds than farm subsidies. If Congress wants to support these farmers and ranchers, conservation programs have an outsized role to play.

Regenerative agriculture funding went down in 2025

EWG found that EQIP obligations to farmers were $1.82 billion across all practices for fiscal year 2025. Of this pot of money, 43%, or $790.6 million, went to farmers for practices that were on EWG’s list of regenerative practices.

Due to the additional funding from the IRA, total EQIP obligations in fiscal year 2024 were $2.6 billion. Of this, $1.88 billion, or 45%, went to practices that were regenerative. Funding for these practices greatly decreased between 2024 and 2025.

Through public records requests, EWG received data for USDA obligations made in 2025. We used data from the USDA’s Financial Assistance Program Data Dashboard(link is external) for 2024 obligations.

Farm bill conservation cuts would hurt farmers

The upcoming farm bill must maintain conservation funding, especially for regenerative practices.

Farmers and ranchers have been promised this money – Congress shouldn’t take it away. The stakes are too high.

Restoring funding for the two USDA programs would not only reduce agriculture’s environmental and climate impact. It could also provide reliable support to tens of thousands of farmers and potentially reduce the costs of ad hoc disaster assistance and crop insurance payouts covered by American taxpayers.

text:
The University of North Carolina at Charlotte (UNC Charlotte) has announced a major expansion to prepare the future U.S. energy workforce and accelerate next-generation research.

Marking a national milestone, UNC Charlotte is establishing a School of Energy inside the William States Lee College of Engineering building. The new school will focus solely on grid modernization and the interdisciplinary hurdles facing the nation's electrical infrastructure.

It builds upon a previously announced $160 million 10-year investment in July by the U.S. National Science Foundation to anchor the Carolinas Solar Energy Innovation Engine.

“Building on the University’s expertise in engineering, the School of Energy brings together perspectives from across disciplines to explore energy challenges in their full complexity,” said Jennifer Troyer, provost at UNC Charlotte, in a statement.

U.S. officials previously selected North Carolina and South Carolina to play an important role in grid modernization and technology deployment under the National Science Foundation (NSF) Regional Innovation Engines program. Across 20 states, 12 regional teams were picked to scale innovation clusters that accelerate the development of critical tech, advancing the U.S. energy economy and sustainability footprint.

For UNC Charlotte, the School of Energy aims to stand out as a four-year career-focused pathway designed to meet these critical industry demands.

“Our strength as an R1 research university, the momentum of the Carolinas Grid Engine and our location in one of the nation’s leading energy hubs give us an extraordinary foundation to build upon," said UNC Charlotte Chancellor Sharon L. Gaber. "Together, we are strengthening Charlotte’s ability to move energy technologies from research to use while preparing the people who will design, build and operate the nation’s next-generation power systems.”

According to a university release, the school’s curriculum will address critical industry areas, including grid automation, transmission-line design and energy-component manufacturing. UNC Charlotte notes these fields are vital to addressing the nation's surging electricity demands driven by the rise of AI data centers, advanced manufacturing and the overall electrification of the U.S. economy.

This engineering-based school aims to establish a centralized hub for the development of academic programs focusing on energy-related topics, spanning grid modernization, policy review and U.S. regulations.

Initial offerings faculty intend to build these new programs on are:

B.S. in Electromechanical Engineering Technology

B.S. in Mechanical Engineering Technology

M.S. in Applied Energy and Electromechanical Engineering

“This structure will empower our students to cross traditional boundaries and lead the charge in revolutionizing a rapidly evolving energy industry,” added Rob Keynton, dean of the William States Lee College of Engineering.

UNC Charlotte's Albert & Freeman Energy Production and Infrastructure Center (EPIC) will serve as the School of Energy's interdisciplinary research arm. Robert Cox, executive director of EPIC and the Duke Energy Distinguished Scholar in Power Engineering Systems, has been named the school’s founding director.

“America’s energy system is facing pressures we have not seen in decades,” said Cox. “Combined with increasingly severe weather and supply chain constraints, these challenges demand new ideas and a workforce prepared to put them into practice.”

Duke Energy, a primary anchor partner for UNC Charlotte's new School of Energy, is also a founding member of the Careers Electric coalition with a heavy focus in North Carolina. While Careers Electric targets trade-level nationwide efforts to scale the electrical workforce, the School of Energy's advanced engineering and technology degrees aim to synchronize a "pipeline" push to address higher-level engineering needs in the U.S.

In North Carolina, Careers Electric claims 70% of licensed electricians are over the age of 50. On a broader scale, employment demand for electrical careers is projected to increase by roughly 10% over the next decade, creating as many as 80,000 job openings each year.

text:
The Washington Suburban Sanitation Commission — the utility company that serves nearly all residents in Montgomery County — is seeking to join a Clean Water Act lawsuit against the District of Columbia and its Water and Sewer Authority (DC Water) stemming from their alleged neglect of the 54-mile Potomac Interceptor sewer line that collapsed in January.

The utility, otherwise known as WSSC Water, said in a statement on Wednesday that it had filed a motion to intervene in the lawsuit. The suit was filed April 20 by the U.S. Justice Department’s Environment and Natural Resources Division in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

“This measure is necessary to allow WSSC Water to directly engage in discussions regarding remedial actions concerning the Potomac Interceptor and related wastewater treatment infrastructure to ensure the viability of that infrastructure for decades to come,” the utility said Wednesday in a statement.

The lawsuit argues that DC Water violated the Clean Water Act and threatened the waterway’s health by failing to “adequately” maintain the interceptor despite knowing for years of extensive corrosion to the pipe and failing to address the collapse itself.

WSSC Water serves nearly 2 million residents in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties, according to the utility’s website. Not all residents in the county receive drinking water from the utility company.

In addition, WSSC Water said that intervening in the lawsuit will give the utility the ability to “engage directly in decisions about costs, future capital improvements and financial responsibilities tied” to the wastewater infrastructure.

The sewer line collapse occurred Jan. 19 just outside of Cabin John on Clara Barton Parkway near I-495. According to DC Water, more than 240 million gallons of raw sewage spewed into the Potomac River, also known as the “nation’s river.”

The interceptor normally carries about 60 million gallons of sewage per day to the Blue Plains Advanced Wastewater Treatment Plant in Southeast D.C., the largest treatment plant in the world.

Though the collapse did not pose a direct threat to drinking water for the county, many residents, environmental advocates and local scientists raised concerns about the damage the spill may have to the river’s ecosystem and aquatic life. In April, the American Rivers environmental advocacy group named the Potomac River the most endangered river in the country.

“The rapid, unchecked buildout of data centers along the Potomac River threatens the drinking water for our nation’s capital and surrounding areas, while a historic sewage spill raises alarms about aging infrastructure,” the advocacy group said in a press release.

The spill also disrupted recreational activities in the area near and downstream from the spill for several months. Island conservation groups, including the Sycamore Island Club and Minnie’s Island Community Conservancy, and Potomac Whitewater Racing Center in Bethesda, adjusted their operations as well as summer and spring schedules to work around the spill.

In the months following the collapse, DC Water officials inspected the sewer line in Cabin John and other stretches of the pipe and identified other areas experiencing extensive corrosion and immediate repair need. Officials said during community meetings after the collapse that the utility had planned repair work to the interceptor this summer but accelerated that timeline in response to the disaster.

Emergency repairs and rehabilitation work are underway in a 175-foot section of the pipe near Pennyfield Lock in Potomac that was showing critical signs of weakness, according to DC Water. As of late July, the utility began adding a new geopolymer lining to the Pennyfield Lock section.

In its statement on Wednesday, WSSC Water noted the emergency repairs in Pennyfield Lock, a section that is two miles upstream from its Potomac Water Filtration Plant. “Our involvement is also critical to protecting our drinking water,” WSSC Water said, adding the plant produces 70% of the drinking water for its customers.

The January collapse occurred about eight miles downstream from WSSC Water’s filtration plant’s intake pumps in Potomac.

“Our priorities are clear: secure reliable wastewater treatment infrastructure, protect our customers’ financial interests, safeguard our drinking water, and ensure our customers have representation in decisions that could have significant and lasting impacts,” WSSC Water said in its statement.

About eight months after the collapse and extensive testing of the water and its sediment, Montgomery County health officials lifted all remaining health advisories for the Potomac River shoreline. Those advisories had been in effect since the collapse of the sewer line in January.

In June, the Potomac Riverkeeper Network, an environmental advocacy and watchdog group, also moved to join the Department of Justice and Environmental Protection Agency lawsuit. The group also conducted independent water quality monitoring of the river.

“We at PRKN had long feared that this disaster was not an accident,” Potomac Riverkeeper Network President Betsy Nicholas said in a June press release about joining the lawsuit.

“It was a failure of decision-making, accountability, and urgency. We, as the voice of the community, must have a seat at the table to assure that paddlers, anglers, outfitters, watermen, and residents — all of whom rely on the Potomac — are made whole and that there is no repeat of this catastrophe,” Nicholas added.
